queue.label: reinvention-mid-career
queue.content:
Changing careers in your forties or fifties is supposed to be reckless. I have done it more than once - finance to beverages, then to building an AI company.

The fear assumes you are starting from zero. You are not. Decades in one field leave you with judgment, pattern recognition, a network, and the ability to read a situation fast.

The best reinventions are not leaps. They are transfers.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/reinvention-mid-career.html

queue.label: nootropics-substance-vs-hype
queue.content:
Nootropic has become one of the most overused words on a beverage label, and increasingly it is applied to products that have not earned it.

The category is not snake oil and it is not magic. Some ingredients have real evidence behind them at real doses, and plenty are there to look good on a panel.

Consumers deserve a clearer way to tell the difference than the front of the can.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/nootropics-substance-vs-hype.html

queue.label: breaking-the-experience-paradox
queue.content:
You cannot get the job without experience, and you cannot get the experience without the job. The longer you look at that, the more absurd it gets.

When talented people cannot break in they tend to blame themselves - not enough hustle, wrong school, bad luck. The barrier is structural, not personal.

Employers de-risk hiring by asking for proof, and the only sanctioned proof has been a prior job. That is the specific problem I built Provieo to solve.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/breaking-the-experience-paradox.html

queue.label: the-second-sip-problem
queue.content:
Almost everyone optimizes for the first sip - the sample table, the bold flavor that has to win a three-second impression.

But nobody builds a daily habit around something they have to tolerate. The flavor that stood out at the table is often the reason the third can is still sitting in the fridge.

Trial measures your marketing. The second purchase measures your product. I have started judging a launch by whether people are quietly still drinking it a month later.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-second-sip-problem.html

queue.label: the-reorder-is-everything
queue.content:
Getting on the shelf feels like the win. It is closer to the invoice arriving.

The shelf is rented, and velocity is the rent. A hundred doors with nothing moving through them teaches a buyer something about you that is hard to unteach. Twenty doors selling through tells the opposite story.

The work most founders think ends at the buyer meeting actually starts there. The reorder is the only yes nobody had to be talked into.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-reorder-is-everything.html

queue.label: protect-the-downside
queue.content:
Twenty-five years in capital markets taught me one thing I still use every day, and it is not how to spot an opportunity.

It is how to size a bet so that being wrong does not end the game. Staying in is worth more than any single trade you get right.

The odd part is that protecting the downside is what lets you be aggressive. Ten small survivable bets with lopsided payoffs beat one heroic wager that has to land.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/protect-the-downside.html

queue.label: the-last-two-weeks
queue.content:
I have learned more about people from their notice period than from any interview I have ever run.

Two colleagues left the same company the same month. One documented every account so the next person could pick it up cold. The other stopped answering email. Nothing in either interview predicted which would be which.

Anyone is diligent when diligence is being graded. The last two weeks are ungraded, which is exactly why they are worth asking a reference about.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-last-two-weeks.html

queue.label: culture-of-ownership
queue.content:
The best teams I have been part of were not the busiest. They were the ones where a small number of people were genuinely on the hook for an outcome.

Lean forces clarity. With no slack to hide in, people stop reporting activity and start owning results - but only if you actually hand over the decision, including the room to get it wrong.

Culture is what you tolerate, not what you put on a wall. Worth getting right before you scale anything else.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/culture-of-ownership.html

queue.label: the-candidate-already-in-the-building
queue.content:
I once ran an expensive outside search for an operations manager, hired him, and watched it come apart within months. The person who eventually did the job well had been on the night shift the whole time, quietly solving three production bottlenecks nobody had assigned.

The bias is not practical, it is psychological. An external hire arrives with a clean story you assemble from a resume and two good conversations, while the person down the hall arrives with a visible record that includes the mistakes - and that record is the only real data you will ever have. Sometimes you genuinely do need a perspective that does not exist inside your walls. That should be a decision you make on purpose, not the thing that happens by default.

So now I ask one question before opening a search: who here is already doing pieces of this work, and has anyone ever asked them directly whether they want it?

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-candidate-already-in-the-building.html

queue.label: the-promotion-nobody-asked-for
queue.content:
I promoted our best regional rep to regional manager. Eight months later he asked to go back to his old job, and we had lost two of the people who had been reporting to him.

My mistake was treating performance as a prediction. Selling well and developing people who sell well draw on almost nothing in common, and I had no evidence he wanted the second one - nobody had ever asked whether he coached his peers or wrote down how he worked. Some of this you genuinely cannot know until someone is in the chair. But the signals we did have were sitting right there, and I did not look at them.

He is back to being one of our best performers, which is the part that still stings: a title was the only reward we had to offer him. A senior individual contributor track would have cost us far less than that promotion did.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-promotion-nobody-asked-for.html

queue.label: the-boomerang-hire
queue.content:
A former colleague emailed last month asking about an opening, and my first reaction was warmth. That reaction is worth almost nothing. I liked working with her; liking someone is not evidence that hiring them a second time is a good decision.

The fair concession is that boomerang hires carry a real advantage. I already know how she works under pressure, how she handles being wrong, how she behaves in the week a launch slips - that is a lot of guessing a stranger would make me do. But it does not answer the only question that matters, which is whether the thing that pushed her out the first time still exists. I rehired someone once into nearly the same role because I missed her. She left inside a year. That was my failure, not hers: I never asked what had changed, in her or in the job.

So I said yes, to a different job - one level up, a new mandate, not a reopened chapter. People change less than we hope and more than we expect, and the only way to tell which you are looking at is to ask a friend the same plain questions you would ask a stranger.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-boomerang-hire.html

queue.label: the-counteroffer-trap
queue.content:
A plant manager of mine resigned with a competing offer about twelve percent above what we were paying him. I matched it, added a little on top, and told myself I had solved the problem. He left anyway, about six months later, on a search he had started by himself.

The honest concession is that a counteroffer is sometimes the right call. When pay has drifted behind the market through plain neglect, matching it is not a bribe, it is correcting your own mistake. My error was treating it as the end of the conversation rather than the start of one I should have had months earlier. The money had been available the whole time. What took a resignation letter to surface was why nobody had asked him to do anything new in a year.

I handled the crisis and skipped the diagnosis, and that is the part I would do differently. Loyalty bought under deadline is never trusted the same way again, by either side. If the first you hear of someone being unhappy is a competing offer, the offer is not the problem.

https://howarddavner.com/insights/the-counteroffer-trap.html
